content: Fuchs' dystrophy is an ocular condition characterized by the gradual degeneration of endothelial cells lining the inner surface of the cornea. This disease typically affects both eyes. Symptoms of Fuchs' Dystrophy: Patients may experience eye pain. There is often increased sensitivity to light, particularly glare. Vision may appear foggy or blurred, especially in the mornings. Individuals may see colored halos around lights. Vision tends to worsen progressively throughout the day. Causes of Fuchs' Dystrophy: The disease targets the endothelium, a thin layer of cells at the back of the cornea. The exact cause of the cell death in the endothelium is unknown. These cells are responsible for pumping excess fluid out of the cornea. As they die, fluid accumulates, leading to corneal swelling and cloudiness. Initially, fluid buildup may occur only during sleep when the eyes are closed. Over time, small blisters may form in the endothelium, which can enlarge and rupture, causing pain. The disease can also alter the shape of the cornea, further impairing vision. Risk Factors: Fuchs' dystrophy can be inherited, often in an autosomal dominant pattern. If one parent has the condition, there is a 50% chance of passing it to their offspring. However, it can also occur in individuals without a family history of the disease. Women are more commonly affected than men. Symptoms typically do not manifest before the age of 50, although early signs may be detectable in individuals in their 30s or 40s. Diagnosis: A slit-lamp examination is used to diagnose Fuchs' dystrophy. Additional diagnostic tests may include: Pachymetry: Measures corneal thickness. Specular microscopy: Examines the endothelial cell layer. Visual acuity testing: Assesses the clarity of vision. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if you experience: Eye pain. Sensitivity to light. A sensation of a foreign object in the eye when none is present. Vision disturbances, such as halos or cloudiness. Progressive worsening of vision. Treatment Options: Eye drops or ointments that reduce corneal fluid can alleviate symptoms. For painful corneal sores, soft contact lenses or surgical procedures to create protective flaps over the sores may help reduce discomfort. The only definitive cure for Fuchs' dystrophy is a corneal transplant. This condition is one of the leading indications for corneal transplantation in the United States. An alternative to traditional corneal transplantation is Deep Lamellar Keratoplasty (DLK), where only the deep layers of the cornea are replaced with donor tissue. This procedure does not require stitches, has a faster recovery time, and carries a lower risk of complications such as rejection. Prognosis: Fuchs' dystrophy is a progressive condition. Without a corneal transplant, severe cases can lead to blindness, significant pain, and profound vision loss. Mild cases may worsen after cataract surgery. Surgeons may assess this risk and adjust surgical techniques or timing accordingly. Potential Complications: Increased sensitivity to light. Vision loss ranging from mild to severe. Frequent and intense pain as the disease advances. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent Fuchs' dystrophy. Avoiding cataract surgery or taking specific precautions during such procedures may help slow the progression of the disease.
